title: The Definite Integral
subtitle: The exact area, as a limit of rectangle sums.

questions.text: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, then $f$ is integrable on $[a, b]$.
questions.explain: Continuous functions always have a definite integral.

questions.text: $int[a,a] f(x) dx =$
questions.explain: No width, no area.

questions.text: $int[b,a] f(x) dx =$
questions.explain: Running backwards flips the sign.

questions.text: What is the difference between $int[0,2] x^2 dx$ and $int x^2 dx$?
options: The first is a number; the second is a family of functions
The first is a function; the second is a number
questions.explain: Definite integrals give numbers (areas). Indefinite integrals give antiderivatives $+ C$.

questions.text: $f(x) = 2x$ on $[-3, 3]$. Which is true?
options: The net signed area is 0 but the total area is 18
questions.explain: Two triangles of area 9, one below the axis: $-9 + 9 = 0$, but total area $9 + 9 = 18$.

questions.text: If $f(x) >= g(x)$ on $[a, b]$, then $int[a,b] f(x) dx >= int[a,b] g(x) dx$.
questions.explain: A taller function has more area under it.

questions.text: $int[a,b] c dx$ for a constant $c$ is
questions.explain: A rectangle of height $c$ and width $b - a$.

questions.text: Which is bigger: $int[3,5] x^2 dx$ or $int[3,5] e^x + 1 dx$?

slides.text:
The **definite integral** is the exact area: the limit of the rectangle sums.
$int[a,b] f(x) dx = lim[n->infty] sum[i=1,n] f(x_i) Delta x$
The $int$ sign is a stretched-out S. S for…
slides.explain: It adds up (sums) infinitely many thin rectangles $f(x) dx$.

slides.text: Area **below** the $x$-axis counts as negative. What is $int[-pi,pi] sin(x) dx$?
slides.hint: The part below the axis exactly cancels the part above.
slides.explain: The two humps are the same size with opposite signs, so they cancel: 0.
